title: Constructing Unrestricted Adversarial Examples with Generative Models
authors: Yang Song, Rui Shu, Nate Kushman, Stefano Ermon

pages.title: Escaping the epsilon-ball threat model
pages.subtitle: Don't perturb a real image, synthesize a fake one

blocks.html: Almost all adversarial-example research lives inside one threat model: take a real image, add a perturbation $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_p \leq \epsilon$ so small it is invisible, and fool the classifier. Defenses are then built and certified against exactly this norm-bounded attack.

This paper points out a blind spot. An attacker is not obligated to start from a real image at all. What if we generate a brand-new image from scratch that is unambiguously, legitimately one class to a human, yet the classifier calls it something else? Such an image is adversarial, but it lives outside any $\epsilon$-ball, so norm-bounded defenses and certificates say nothing about it.

We propose unrestricted adversarial examples: inputs that are not constrained to be near any clean image, generated from scratch with a conditional generative model, yet still legitimate members of a class while being misclassified.
The threat is arguably more dangerous because it sidesteps the entire defensive apparatus the community had built around small perturbations.
The classic restricted attack searches for a perturbation within a tiny ball around a fixed clean image $x$:
Read this as: 'nudge $x$ just enough to break $f$, but not enough for a human to notice.' The smallness of $\delta$ is what guarantees the true label has not changed.
An unrestricted adversarial example drops the $\epsilon$ constraint entirely. Instead of anchoring to a real image, it asks for any image at all that satisfies two conditions:

items: A human oracle confidently assigns it the true class $y$ (it really looks like a valid example of $y$).
The classifier $f$ assigns it a different class (it is misclassified).

blocks.html: Because there is no proximity constraint, the search space is the entire space of realistic images of class $y$, not a thin shell around one photo. The challenge becomes: how do we stay inside the set of realistic, correctly-labeled images while hunting for misclassification?

pages.title: Search the latent space of a GAN
pages.subtitle: Let the generator keep images realistic

blocks.html: The key tool is a conditional generative model (an AC-GAN) trained to produce realistic images of a given class from a latent code $z$. Because the generator $G$ only ever outputs realistic, on-manifold images, optimizing over $z$ keeps every candidate looking like a genuine image, no perturbation budget required.

To craft an unrestricted adversarial example of source class $y$, we search the latent space for a code whose generated image is realistic and clearly class $y$ to humans, yet fools the target classifier $f$. The optimization combines three pulls:

items: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}$ pushes the target classifier $f$ toward the wrong class (this is what makes it adversarial).
$\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ uses the GAN's own auxiliary classifier to keep the image firmly looking like the true class $y$, so a human still reads it correctly.
$\|z - z_0\|^2$ keeps the code near a well-formed starting point $z_0$ so the generator outputs a clean, realistic image rather than a degenerate one.

blocks.html: By optimizing in latent space rather than pixel space, every step yields a realistic image. The generator is the guardrail that keeps us on the manifold of legitimate examples.

pages.title: Keeping the human label honest
pages.subtitle: Why these aren't just mislabeled garbage

blocks.html: The whole claim hinges on the generated image truly belonging to class $y$ for a human. The auxiliary loss term and the latent-proximity term work together to ensure the image stays a confident, recognizable member of $y$. The authors validate this with human studies: annotators are shown the generated images and reliably label them as the intended class, confirming the examples are legitimate, not ambiguous noise.

So the result is a clean separation of opinion: humans say $y$, the classifier says not-$y$. That is the definition of an adversarial example, achieved without ever touching a real photograph or staying within any norm ball.

Norm-bounded defenses, including adversarial training and certified methods like PixelDP, all reason about a neighborhood around a fixed input. An unrestricted example has no such anchor, so those guarantees simply do not apply to it.

The authors demonstrate that models hardened against $\epsilon$-bounded attacks remain vulnerable to unrestricted ones, and that these examples often transfer across different classifiers. Robustness in the restricted sense gives a false sense of security against this broader attack surface.

pages.title: A broader definition of robustness
pages.subtitle: What the field has to grapple with

blocks.html: This paper enlarges the question from 'is the model stable near real images?' to 'can the model be fooled by any realistic, correctly-labeled image?' The latter is much harder to defend against and much closer to what a real adversary could do.

items: Adversarial examples need not be perturbations of real data; generative models can synthesize them from scratch.
Latent-space search keeps generated images realistic and human-correct, sidestepping the epsilon-ball entirely.
Norm-based defenses and certificates do not cover this threat model.
Motivated later community efforts (the Unrestricted Adversarial Examples challenge) to build defenses against this broader class.

blocks.html: The enduring message: true robustness must mean agreeing with humans on all realistic inputs, not just resisting tiny pixel nudges around a test set.
